title: Managing weaner pigs in cold weather
subtitle: Keeping freshly weaned pigs warm, eating, and growing during a cold snap.
excerpt: Weaner pigs are at their most vulnerable to cold in the two weeks immediately after weaning, when they are adjusting to solid food and no longer benefit from the sow's body heat. A chilled weaner stops eating, loses weight, and becomes susceptible to disease. The fixes are straightforward: adequate bedding, a draught-free creep area, and a feeding routine that encourages prompt eating. Getting these right keeps the weaning dip shallow.
sourceNotes: AHDB Pork, Weaner pig management (2022). NPA, Smallholder Pig Keeping Guide (2022). John Gadd, Pig Production Problems (2011), 5m Books, chapter on post-weaning management. DEFRA Code of Recommendations for the Welfare of Pigs (2003, updated guidance 2023).

glossaryTerms.definition: The temporary reduction in growth rate that occurs in the first one to two weeks after weaning. All piglets experience some weaning dip; its depth and duration depend on weaning age, diet transition management, stress levels, and environmental temperature.

A small, enclosed warm resting space within a pig pen, accessible only to small pigs rather than adults. In post-weaning management, a creep provides a draught-free, well-bedded retreat that helps small pigs maintain body temperature.

content.text: Newly weaned pigs at 28 days old need an ambient temperature of around 27 degrees Celsius to remain comfortable without huddling. By 8 weeks they are comfortable at 22 degrees, and by 12 weeks at 18 degrees. In a UK winter, the gap between these targets and the ambient temperature in an unheated building is often 15 to 25 degrees. Bridging that gap with bedding, draught exclusion, and a
is the practical route to minimising the

Deep straw bedding is the most effective, lowest-cost way to keep weaner pigs warm. A minimum of 200 mm of fresh wheat or barley straw in the sleeping area on weaning day, with additional straw added as it compresses or dampens, gives pigs an effective nesting environment. Weaners will burrow into deep straw and create a microclimate several degrees warmer than the surrounding air.
Cold air moving across the pen at pig height is more damaging than low ambient temperature. Block gaps under doors, between boards, and around fittings at pig level.
Keep ventilation above pig height: stale air and ammonia cause breathing problems just as cold does.
Hang a curtain (a canvas sack or heavy rubber mat) over the creep entrance to block draughts without blocking ventilation.

A 175 or 250 watt infrared lamp in a guarded fitting, hung 600 to 700 mm above the creep floor, adds useful warmth to the resting area. Keep it high enough that pigs cannot reach the fitting. Lower it if pigs avoid the space beneath it; raise it if they huddle under it all the time.

Offer weaner pellets little and often for the first five days rather than ad-lib. Newly weaned pigs can overeat one large meal and develop gut problems. Feed small handfuls two or three times daily, fresh each time. This works better than a full hopper.
Add a small amount of warm water or milk to weaner pellets for the first two days: this bridges the gap from sow milk to dry feed.
Keep water nipples or drinkers at a height the weaners can reach comfortably without stretching. Pigs that cannot drink freely will not eat.

attrs.cue: Weaners huddled in a pile in the corner, not eating
attrs.fix: Add more straw immediately. Check for draught at pig level with a strip of light paper. Turn on the heat lamp if not already in use. If pigs do not begin to move and eat within two hours of improving the environment, there may be an underlying health issue.

attrs.cue: Yellow-grey watery scour in weaners two to five days after weaning
attrs.cause: Post-weaning diarrhoea from E. coli, compounded by stress and diet change
attrs.fix: Ensure water is freely available; dehydration worsens scour rapidly. Discuss treatment with your vet. Post-weaning E. coli scour in a pig herd on a known farm is a vet-prescription product situation, not an improvise-and-hope one.
